stem: Find the local maxima or local minima of \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working carries four corrupted lines, although its final answers (maximum \(2\) at \(x = -1\), minimum \(-2\) at \(x = 1\)) are correct. (1) A stray \(\Rightarrow 0\) appears mid-chain in \(x^2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 1\). (2) "\(f'(x) > 0\) for \(x = 1 - h \Rightarrow f(x)\) is decreasing for \(x > 1\)" contradicts the line above it, which correctly derives \(f'(1 - h) < 0\); it should read \(f'(x) < 0\), decreasing for \(x < 1\). (3) The mirrored line for \(x = 1 + h\) carries the same defect. (4) "\(f'(x) > 0\) for \(-1 < x < -1 + h\)" should be \(< 0\); as printed, both intervals around \(x = -1\) show \(> 0\), which would make \(x = -1\) not a maximum at all. The working is preserved below as printed.]

Given that \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\) ... (I)
Differentiate (I) \(w.\ r.\ t.\ x\).
\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1)\) ... (II)
For extreme values, \(f'(x) = 0\)
\(3x^2 - 3 = 0\) i.e. \(3(x^2 - 1) = 0\)
i.e. \(x^2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\)
The turning points are \(x = 1\) and \(x = -1\)
Let's consider the turning point, \(x = 1\)
Let \(x = 1 - h\) for a small, \(h > 0\), from (II) we get,
\(f'(1 - h) = 3[(1 - h)^2 - 1] = 3(1 - 2h + h^2 - 1) = 3h(h - 2)\)
\(\therefore\) \(f'(1 - h) < 0\) ... [since, \(h > 0\), \(h - 2 < 0\)]
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) for \(x = 1 - h \Rightarrow f(x)\) is decreasing for, \(x > 1\).
Now for \(x = 1 + h\) for a small, \(h > 0\), from (II) we get,
\(f'(1 + h) = 3[(1 + h)^2 - 1] = 3(1 + 2h + h^2 - 1) = 3(h^2 + 2h)\)
\(\therefore\) \(f'(1 + h) > 0\) ... [since, \(h > 0\), \(h^2 + 2h > 0\)]
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) < 0\) for \(x = 1 + h \Rightarrow f(x)\) is increasing for, \(x < 1\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) < 0\) for \(1 - h < x < 1\)
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) for \(1 < x < 1 + h\).
\(\therefore\) \(x = 1\) is the point of local minima.
Minima of \(f(x)\), is \(f(1) = 1^3 - 3(1) = -2\)
Now, let's consider the turning point, \(x = -1\)
Let \(x = -1 - h\) for a small, \(h > 0\), from (II) we get,
\(\therefore\) \(f'(-1 - h) = 3[(-1 - h)^2 - 1] = 3(1 + 2h + h^2 - 1) = 3(h^2 + 2h)\)
\(\therefore\) \(f'(-1 - h) > 0\) ... [since, \(h > 0\), \(h^2 + 2h > 0\)]
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) for \(x = -1 - h \Rightarrow f(x)\) is increasing for, \(x < -1\).
Now for \(x = -1 + h\) for a small, \(h > 0\), from (II) we get,
\(\therefore\) \(f'(-1 + h) = 3[(-1 + h)^2 - 1] = 3(1 - 2h + h^2 - 1) = -3h(2 - h)\)
\(\therefore\) \(f'(-1 + h) < 0\) ... [since, \(h > 0\), \(2 - h > 0\)]
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) < 0\) for \(x = -1 + h \Rightarrow f(x)\) is decreasing for, \(x > -1\).
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) for \(-1 - h < x < -1\)
\(\therefore\) \(f'(x) > 0\) for \(-1 < x < -1 + h\).
\(\therefore\) \(x = -1\) is the point of local maxima.
Maxima of \(f(x)\), is \(f(-1) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2\)
Hence, Maxima of \(f(x)\) is 2 and Minima of \(f(x)\) is \(-2\)
